extracted.intended_audience: geologists, coal-measure specialists, and mining engineers interested in coal-swamp physiography and seam structure
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for interpreting Coal Measures (coal-seams, split-seams, wash-outs, cleat) from field observations, boreholes, and analogies with modern swamps; includes experimental-reporting notes for optical-rotation work on crystals. Intended for geological field/mapping and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental specification for optical-handedness determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important to know the exact conditions of the experiment whenever the question of the correct discrimination of right- or left-handedness in the optical rotation of crystals is being dealt with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify whether the experiment is a projection experiment or a table polariscope (projection inverts the picture, producing apparent reversal); adopt and state the Biot convention for directional (right- or left-handed) designation; where possible cut the section-plate from a crystal which is clearly a single individual (not a twin) showing characteristic faces; avoid ambiguous phrasing such as 'from the point of view of the observer looking in the same direction as the light is being propagated' when only colour of field-centre is referred to; amend inadequate footnotes to state conventions explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics defining a 'true' coal-seam
rubrics_metrics.description: True coal-seams are characterised by: (1) Wide extent. (2) Uniformity of thickness and character over extensive areas. (3) Freedom from intermingled detrital mineral matter. (4) Constant presence of a seat-earth or rootlet bed. (5) Entire absence of remains of aquatic animals within the seam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these five diagnostic features to distinguish true coal-seams from cannel (where positives/negatives reverse). Apply them when assessing whether a seam is autochthonous (growth-in-place) versus allochthonous (drift).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and interpretation of split-seams
rubrics_metrics.description: A split-seam is the intercalation into the midst of the coal of a wedge of sandstone, shale, or the like so that the seam becomes subdivided by intervening strata into two or more seams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider Bowman's 'sag' (local floor sag and drowning then siltation) but also differential shrinkage of peat versus deposited sand/mud as a mechanism; observe whether upper element is arched while floor remains flat (supports differential-shrinkage model). Use the plano-convex lens mental model: an infilled channel initially convex downward may appear convex upward after peat-to-coal contraction. Investigate analogous cases and expect arching if shrinkage explanation holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field method for tracing seam interruptions and mapping anomalies
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic exploration (follow the bottom coal, track upper element trends) and borehole proofing can trace interruptions and map them continuously for long distances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When thin intercalations thicken and coal elements disappear, follow the bottom/top coals and use boreholes to confirm presence/absence above or below partings; trace margins along traverses and map interruptions over miles; use multiple transverse explorations to establish geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria to distinguish erosional 'wash-outs' from tectonic faulting or thrusting
rubrics_metrics.description: Wash-outs (deep erosions) should produce loss of coal that is not balanced by equivalent duplication elsewhere; tectonic thrusts/flat-sharing faults would predict no net loss of coal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure thicknesses and breadths: if a barren gap of coal (e.g., 210 ft) is only compensated by a much smaller excess (e.g., 35 ft) at margins, this indicates genuine loss (erosion) rather than mere duplication by faulting. Also examine regional alignment: wash-outs aligned in multiple principal directions (N.E.—S.W., N.W.—S.E., N.—S., E.—W.) argue against a single-direction tectonic thrust cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seismic-origin indicators in seam disturbances
rubrics_metrics.description: Disturbances such as stretching, breaking, lurching, rolling/heaving of sand beds, shaking to pulp of muddy deposits, rending/heaving of peat, cracks infilled with extraneous material, and inverted cones ('dog's-teeth', 'paps', or 'drops') are diagnostic of earthquake action on unconsolidated alluvial deposits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for unstratified argillaceous masses (consolidated sludge-like material), nearly vertical ragged edges of seams against such masses, sand-blows, sand-filled fissures containing lignite, and surface features analogous to those produced by known earthquakes (Sylhet, New Madrid). Infer seismic lurching when these subterranean and surface signatures co-occur; expect permanent deformation (wrinkles, sag, ridge) and injection phenomena (sand into overlying strata).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic features and provenance implications of cleat (slynes) in coal
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleat is a well-developed system of joints (not like slate cleavage), present at all scales (from jth-of-an-inch flakes to tree-trunk-size), usually disposed at characteristic directions (overwhelming N.W.-S.E. in the Northern Hemisphere; N.E.-S.W. tendency in many southern coals), and often developed prior to jointing of associated measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cleat orientation and spacing as a field diagnostic (e.g., cleat at ~35° to length of some leaves, intervals as small as j,th of an inch). Observe that cleat is independent of joints in shales/sandstones (implies early development due to peat contraction during lignitization). Collect global cleat-direction data; absence of cleat in anthracite is meaningful. Consider directive continuous strains (tidal or planetary influences) as possible causes of consistent directional tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources-of-ash framework for coal and implications for interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ash of coal may be composed of three distinct materials: (1) mineral substances belonging to plant-tissues; (2) detrital mineral substances washed or blown into the area of growing peat; (3) sparry minerals located in the lumen of the cleat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that sparry veins in cleat (carbonates, iron sulphides) can be major contributors to ash; these veins likely introduced by percolation from overlying measures after cleat formation. Hence variations in ash content do not reliably indicate different plant constituents; washing and removal of heavy mineral particles can reduce ash to levels comparable with anthracite. Evaluate ash origin before inferring botanical differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive rule: use modern swamp/delta analogues for ancient Coal Measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Each Coal Measure fact finds its illustration in modern swamps and deltas; modern examples exemplify features seen in ancient coal-swamps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invert the comparative method: not only compare ancient to modern, but use characteristic modern swamp phenomena to explain ancient stratigraphic features (split-seams, wash-outs, sand-blows, cleat formation). This supports autochthonous growth-in-place interpretations of many coal seams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and interpretation of 'proud coal' and seam duplications
rubrics_metrics.description: Proud coal regions where the seam swells to two or three times its normal thickness may arise from repetition of the whole seam or of its upper part, by shearing or overfolding; such violent displacement and over-ridings are unlike displacement produced by faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume all swellings/duplications are due to tectonic thrusting—localisation to a single stratigraphical plane and patterns of occurrence contradict simple thrust explanations. Consider mechanisms such as shearing, overfolding, or differential deposition and post-depositional processes when explaining proud coal.
